claims.text: High-entropy alloys generally contain at least five principal elements in near-equimolar proportions.
The target high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have a homogeneous, random atomic distribution of their constituent metals.
The relevant nanoparticles are spherical and 5–50 nm in diameter.
High configurational entropy creates a more uniform atomic bonding environment in alloy nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy produces distributed, homogeneous lattice strain at nanoparticle surfaces.
A uniform distribution of interatomic interactions minimizes local surface-energy imbalances.
Uniform interactions and distributed surface strain increase the cohesive-energy barrier to atomic disordering.
The increased cohesive-energy barrier delays formation of a premelted surface layer.
Binary and ternary nanoparticles possess localized compositional heterogeneities that nucleate early surface premelting.
High-entropy nanoparticles have a higher whole-particle melting temperature than comparable binary or ternary nanoparticles.
The controlled comparison should use high-entropy and binary or ternary nanoparticles matched for size and morphology and synthesized under otherwise identical conditions.
Both groups should undergo the same thermal ramp under an inert atmosphere, with DSC and in situ high-resolution TEM used to monitor melting and surface disordering.
Use of an inert or controlled atmosphere minimizes oxidation-related effects on the thermal response.
Relative to the binary or ternary control, high-entropy nanoparticles will show a statistically significant delay in surface-premelting onset.
The proposed entropy-dependent behavior holds over the 5–50 nm particle-size range.
The thermal response may differ for much larger particles or when surface modifications dominate.
The magnitude of the premelting-temperature shift depends on the elemental combination and processing details.
The hypothesis is falsified if the high-entropy group shows neither a statistically significant premelting delay nor a higher melting temperature under identical conditions.
